metadata.title: Dirac's theorem on chordal graphs implies Brooks' theorem

nodes.name: Proper $k$-coloring
nodes.statement: A (proper) $k$-coloring of $G$ is a function $\varphi: V(G) \rightarrow \{1, \dots, k\}$ such that $\varphi(u) \neq \varphi(v)$ if $uv \in E(G)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A k-coloring assigns one of k colors to each vertex so that adjacent vertices receive distinct colors.

nodes.name: List assignment
nodes.statement: A list assignment of a graph is a function $L$ that assigns to each vertex $v$ a list $L(v)$ of colors.

nodes.name: $L$-colorable
nodes.statement: The graph $G$ is $L$-colorable if it has a proper coloring $f$ such that $f(v) \in L(v)$ for each vertex $v$ of $G$.

nodes.name: Chordal graph
nodes.statement: A graph is chordal if every chordless cycle of the graph is a triangle.

nodes.name: Perfect elimination ordering
nodes.statement: A perfect elimination ordering of a graph $G$ is an ordering $v_1, \dots, v_n$ of $V(G)$ such that, for each $i \in [n]$, the graph induced by $\{v_j: j < i, v_iv_j \in E(G)\}$ is a clique.

nodes.name: Brooks' Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\Delta \geq 3$ be an integer. Then every connected graph $G \neq K_{\Delta+1}$ with maximum degree $\Delta$ has a $\Delta$-coloring.

nodes.name: Dirac's Theorem on Chordal Graphs
nodes.statement: A graph is chordal if, and only if, it admits a perfect elimination ordering.
conclusions: $G$ is chordal $\iff$ $G$ admits a perfect elimination ordering

nodes.name: List-coloring of chordal graphs by clique number
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a chordal graph with clique number $\omega$. Let $L$ be a list assignment of $G$ such that $|L(v)| \geq \omega$ for each $v \in V(G)$. Then $G$ has an $L$-coloring.
assumptions: $G$ is a chordal graph with clique number $\omega$
$L$ is a list assignment of $G$ with $|L(v)| \geq \omega$ for each $v \in V(G)$

nodes.name: List-color Brooks' Theorem (Vizing; Erdős–Rubin–Taylor)
nodes.statement: Let $\Delta \geq 3$ and let $G \neq K_{\Delta+1}$ be a connected graph with maximum degree $\Delta$. If $L$ is a list assignment of $G$ with $|L(v)| \geq \Delta$ for each $v \in V(G)$, then $G$ has an $L$-coloring.
assumptions: $G \neq K_{\Delta+1}$ is a connected graph with maximum degree $\Delta$
$L$ is a list assignment with $|L(v)| \geq \Delta$ for each $v \in V(G)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1 (greedy on perfect elimination ordering)
nodes.statement: Greedy coloring along a perfect elimination ordering: each uncolored vertex has fewer already-colored neighbors than $|L(v)|$, so a list-color choice always exists.

nodes.name: Proof of List-color Brooks' Theorem
nodes.statement: Take a minimum counterexample $G$; by Lemma 1 it is not chordal, so it has a chordless cycle of length $\geq 4$. Build two modified graphs $F, H$, show one avoids $K_{\Delta+1}$, color it by minimality, then extend the coloring along the cycle to a contradiction.

nodes.name: Pick perfect elimination ordering
nodes.statement: Let $v_1, \dots, v_n$ be a perfect elimination ordering of $G$ (exists by Dirac's theorem since $G$ is chordal).

nodes.name: Greedy color in order
nodes.statement: Color the vertices of $G$ greedily in the order $v_1, \dots, v_n$: at each $v$, the already-colored neighbors form a clique of size $< \omega \leq |L(v)|$, so a free color in $L(v)$ remains.

nodes.name: Take minimum counterexample
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a counterexample with $|V(G)|$ as small as possible.

nodes.name: $G$ is not chordal
nodes.statement: By Lemma 1, $G$ is not chordal, since otherwise $|L(v)| \geq \Delta \geq \omega(G)$ would give an $L$-coloring.

nodes.name: Pick a chordless cycle and form $F$, $H$
nodes.statement: Take a chordless cycle $C = x_1 x_2 \dots x_k x_1$ with $k \geq 4$; set $F = G - (C - \{x_1,x_2,x_3\}) + (x_1,x_3)$ and $H = G - (C - \{x_2,x_3,x_4\}) + (x_2,x_4)$.

nodes.name: One of $F$, $H$ avoids $K_{\Delta+1}$
nodes.statement: If both $F$ and $H$ contained a $K_{\Delta+1}$, the neighbors of $x_2$ outside $C$ would be pairwise adjacent and adjacent to $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$, exceeding the degree bound $\Delta$; so WLOG $F$ has no $K_{\Delta+1}$.

nodes.name: Color $F$ by minimality
nodes.statement: Let $L'$ be the restriction of $L$ to $V(F)$. By the minimality of the counterexample, $F$ has an $L'$-coloring $f$.

nodes.name: Define residual lists $L^*$ on $C$
nodes.statement: Let $L^*(x_i) = L(x_i) \setminus \{f(u): (u, x_i) \in E(G) - E(C)\}$ for $i \in [k]$. Then $|L^*(x_i)| \geq 2$ for all $i$.

nodes.name: Choose $c_1 \in L^*(x_1)$ leaving $\geq 2$ options at $x_2$
nodes.statement: If $|L^*(x_1)| = |L^*(x_2)| = |L^*(x_3)| = 2$, the lists are not pairwise equal (else $f$ would not exist on the triangle $x_1 x_2 x_3 \subset F$); WLOG pick $c_1 \in L^*(x_1)$ with $|L^*(x_2) \setminus \{c_1\}| \geq 2$.

nodes.name: Extend coloring around $C$ to a contradiction
nodes.statement: Color $x_1 \mapsto c_1$, $x_k \mapsto c_k \in L^*(x_k) \setminus \{c_1\}$, then for $i = k-1,\dots,3$ pick $c_i \in L^*(x_i) \setminus \{c_{i+1}\}$, and finally $c_2 \in L^*(x_2) \setminus \{c_1, c_3\}$ ($\geq 2$ options remain). This extends $f$ to an $L$-coloring of $G$, contradicting that $G$ was a counterexample.
